q: Wave can undergo reflection, refraction and diffraction.
e: These are the three fundamental behaviors of waves when encountering boundaries or obstacles.

q: These phenomena are usually studied by means of water wave in a ripple tank.
e: A ripple tank is the standard apparatus for visualizing these wave properties.

q: The ripple tank is a convenient piece of apparatus for demonstrating the properties of waves.
e: It allows for clear observation of wavefronts and their interactions.

q: Wavefront: The surface that joins all the points of same phase is called wavefront.
e: This is the precise definition of a wavefront.

q: Reflection: When a series of wave strike an obstacle, they are turned back.
e: This describes the basic mechanism of wave reflection.

q: This turning back of waves is called refraction of waves.
e: This turning back of waves is called reflection of waves.

q: This turning back of waves is called reflection of waves.
e: Reflection is the correct term for waves bouncing back from an obstacle.

q: When waves strike a straight barrier, the waves are reflected from the barrier.
e: This is a standard example of wave reflection.

q: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
e: This is the law of reflection, which applies to waves.

q: The wavelength and velocity of the wave change in reflection of wave.
e: The wavelength and velocity of the wave remain constant in reflection of wave.

q: The wavelength and velocity of the wave remain constant in reflection of wave.
e: Only the direction changes; speed and wavelength are preserved in the same medium.

q: Refraction: The speed of water waves depends on the depth of water.
e: Water depth is the primary factor affecting water wave speed in a ripple tank.

q: It increases when the depth of water becomes less deep.
e: It decreases when the depth of water becomes less deep.

q: It decreases when the depth of water becomes less deep.
e: Shallower water causes water waves to slow down.

q: When water waves pass from deep to shallow water the velocity of wave is lesser and the wavelength is shorter or vice-versa.
e: This accurately describes the changes in velocity and wavelength during refraction.

q: When waves are incident to the boundary with an angle, the direction of the waves changes.
e: This change in direction is the defining characteristic of refraction.

q: Such a change in direction is called diffraction.
e: Such a change in direction is called refraction.

q: Such a change in direction is called refraction.
e: Refraction is the bending of waves due to a change in speed.

q: It can be noticed that in refraction, the wavelength and velocity change but frequency remains the same.
e: Frequency is determined by the source and does not change during refraction.

q: It can be noticed that in refraction, the frequency changes but wavelength and velocity remain the same.
e: In refraction, the wavelength and velocity change but frequency remains the same.

q: Diffraction: Diffraction is the spreading of waves from the straight-on direction through a gap (or) moves around an obstacle.
e: This is the standard definition of wave diffraction.

q: The wave that passes the edges of the gap of the obstacle spread out.
e: This spreading is the observable effect of diffraction.

q: The wider the gap, the more the waves spread out.
e: The wider the gap, the less the waves spread out.

q: The wider the gap, the less the waves spread out.
e: Significant diffraction only occurs when the gap size is comparable to the wavelength.

q: The narrower the gap, the more the waves spread out.
e: A narrower gap relative to the wavelength causes more pronounced spreading.

q: Note that the wavelength does not change in diffraction.
e: Diffraction changes the direction and shape of the wavefront, but not its wavelength.

q: Diffraction around an obstacle includes radio waves that are diffracted as they pass over the hill.
e: This is a real-world example of wave diffraction.
